utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Well, technical problems have been resolved, or did they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, with the assistance of the Prosecution, we're able to do what we wanted to be able to do. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I do understand that you made a list of questions, quite a long list. May I take it that you wanted to draw the attention of Defence counsel to this list of questions so to see whether they could include those in the examination? Because the rule is any additional questions, first consult with counsel, and then if that's -- and then questions to be put to the witness, which is you yourself at this moment. May I take it that you first want the counsel to have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. However, there will be other questions, too, and I didn't have time to write them up because my time was so short. I do apologise because I made so many mistakes, as I had to write this quickly, but I did this on the basis of what I agreed upon yesterday with the lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think the obvious course to take is to provide it to you, Mr. Stewart, and to see whether you can decipher it, perhaps with the assistance of Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour. No doubt about it, Your Honour, I'm going to need it absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll return it, Mr. Registrar, one copy to be provided to the Defence. I take it that if the Prosecution would like to look at the document in order to satisfy itself that these are questions suggested by Mr. Krajisnik -- but if you want to receive a copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'd appreciate that, Your Honour. We certainly take the Court's assurance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, I can't give any assurance. It's finally -- Mr. Krajisnik presents what he says is a list of questions to Mr. Stewart. I'm not in a position to verify that, but if you would consider that -- we will keep one copy, at least, so that if there's any dispute about whether this is hidden correspondence or whether it's really a list of questions, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's probably a suitable safe-guard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Probably in the spirit of the way we deal with things, my assurance, based on what Mr. Sladojevic tells me, will go a long way, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can Mr. Stewart adjust his microphone. The interpreters cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope it's been adjusted in the right way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you're invited to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Krajisnik once I've reminded Mr. Krajisnik that he is still bound by his solemn declaration he gave when he started his testimony -- but you're raising your hand, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through your secretary I asked for a favour. I don't know whether it will be conveyed to you. Would you like me to tell you what it's about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that's -- yes. We have been informed about it, and we have to check with our agendas. Is there any day -- it's about -- perhaps I could say it in public. It's about the possibility to see the dentist somewhere next week, which would delay, most likely, the start of that day. We have to look in our agendas first. Is there any specific day on which you would have an opportunity to see the dentist? Yes, I see it should be Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday, between 8.00 and 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at it and we'll inform you as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution have offered to play the CD which was introduced a long time ago, which is P70, P7-0. It's not the whole thing we need, to remind Your Honours, because it's been in evidence, but it's a clip which includes a passage where Mr. Krajisnik is standing in front of a map. It's from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remember the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour will remember it, but I would -- it's unusual, of course, to be wanting to play again something already played, but Your Honour will see that there is an obvious reason for doing that in this case. And we have the transcript of this, Your Honour. It's P70 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's been received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- if Your Honours have that. And I've got -- oh, Mr. Krajisnik has it as well. I don't know whether anybody's getting any sort of sound at all. Sorry, is anybody getting any sound? I see shaking heads. So -- Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sound is gone again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it was rather short-lived, wasn't it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we play it and see whether we get sound now? Yes, the volume is at maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose I could say, Your Honour, that if nobody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sound again is not there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber, including nobody else, including Mr. Krajisnik, feels not greatly disadvantaged, it's for the soundtrack I'm playing it. We have the transcript and we've played it before. It's important for the visuals to see it, the map there, and see what we're talking about. That's what it's about, Your Honour. I'm not fussed, Your Honour, about getting the sound if nobody else is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed. The picture is still of a younger Mr. Krajisnik, if I remember. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we're all in that position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, first of all -- it may be that we need to play on just to see you -- there's some point, we know, where you lift up -- there's an overlay on this map. I think we need to see that happen. We've got you back where --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, for practical purposes, that's really all we need to see, then. We can look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, the -- you remember this and you've seen it before anyway in court. This was in 1992. We do know that much. Do you remember yourself exactly when it was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this was 1992. At least, that's what I think. Because there was no such map in 1992. But never mind, that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's not insignificant, Mr. Krajisnik. If you can do your best to remember -- well, as best you can when it was, but you can't say any more than you don't think that it was 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was no such map in 1992. There was Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, and so on. All right. I say this with a degree of reservation. Perhaps this map had been drawn, and perhaps this was not the actual state of affairs. This was what was held by our troops. That's what the text says, but that was not the situation in 1992. They didn't hold Gorazde, Zepa, or Srebrenica; none of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the map that's underneath the overlay on that video, Mr. Krajisnik, is that either exactly the same as one of the maps that we have here in court or which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the OTP has the original, the big map, whereas we have the small map, bluish-green, if I can put it that way; blue, green, and yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, so it's -- sorry, I'm just retrieving it. It's the map that -- well, we've got it at --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the same one you used for your markings the other day.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just bigger, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've forgotten the number for a moment -- is it 293? Yes, 293. Thank you, Mr. Haider. P293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first clarify the date. Mr. Krajisnik, you said it's not 1992. Would it be later? Would it be earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when it was, but I would like to draw your attention to this, the attention of the Trial Chamber, to what it says here, Momcilo Krajisnik, where it says: This is held by the Army of Republika Srpska, these borders. But those were not the borders in 1992. So I saw that, I noticed that. I guess this would be 1995 or I don't know what year. In all fairness, Gorazde isn't there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's, Mr. Krajisnik, have a -- I don't know whether you've had a chance to read the text again recently, but the -- let's go through it. "We are standing in front of the ethnic map of former Bosnia and Herzegovina with marked borders of the territory that is presently possessed by the Bosnian Serb army." And that's the overlay - is that right? - that we see. The marked borders there, we can see those, can we, on that map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is the map underneath the foil. What we see here is a foil.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What we're seeing on the screen, Mr. Krajisnik, at the moment, that is showing, is it, the marked borders of the territory that, at the time you were speaking, you were saying was presently possessed by the Bosnian Serb army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the text says, that what we see here is what was held by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And does that -- that being at the time you were speaking, what you were saying was held by the Bosnian Serb army, how accurately, if at all, does that enable you to date this presentation that we see on the video?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this interview and everything I said. I can give my comments on this, but I cannot pin-point the time. What struck me now was that in 1992 neither Srebrenica nor Zepa were marked, at least, and those were enclaves in 1992. And Gorazde was not marked either. So this brings me to this dilemma as to when this interview was actually filmed. However, I can give you my comments on the entire interview right now. This wouldn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we'll take it point by point, Mr. Krajisnik, and then you can, no doubt, sweep up any comments. You -- after saying what the map is, you say: "I can only say that what was being said, that we are possessing the territories ethnically populated by the other national communities, that is not true, which can be seen on the ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which we can cover with the transparent sheet on which the territories are exactly marked, which is possessed by our army, that those are in fact areas that belong to our people." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, it's a simple observation to make and it can be seen by anybody looking at the maps, that the map P293, if one compares it with the territory -- and it's -- the -- of course it's that swathe of outer territory on this map we see on the screen, which is the territory you're saying is held by the Bosnian Serb army, it's clear that that territory, as on that overlay, does include, according to P93 [sic], quite a number of areas of land which are marked as majority populated by other ethnic groups. And I see you're nodding. You seem to accept that basic point so far. So the question is: How does that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- reconcile with what you're saying in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm grateful for the fact that this question is on our agenda because it is on my list of questions. If we were to hear the soundtrack, at one point we would see that the tape breaks down and then there is a continuation precisely when I was giving that answer, that we are holding only our own territory. I mean, you cannot say that in the eastern part of the territory, the scarcely populated territory is majority Muslim territory. The sentence that is missing from the text and which I did utter then was: There are more Serbs in Sarajevo that we are prepared to cede to the Muslim side than in all of the eastern part, the sparsely populated part, than there are Muslims in that sparsely populated part. I know exactly how I was explaining all of this because this had to do with an ethnic map. And of course, in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are many very small settlements, and then if you were to add all of them up, there are more Serbs in the centre of Muslim Sarajevo, the Sarajevo that would belong to them, than in -- than there are Muslims in all of these towns from Trebinje to Zvornik. Perhaps the map isn't exactly right, but that would be it, more or less. So that was the explanation I provided when I was explaining this map, and I said that we had envisaged some enclaves in this territory of ours. Well, it's not exactly drawn here, but in all negotiations we thought about these enclaves, Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, and so on. That's the core of the matter, and that is why I wish we could have heard the soundtrack of this video clip. I saw exactly where the tape was broken off. I don't know whether somebody did this intentionally or unintentionally, but that could have been heard and I can tell you exactly where it was and where this one sentence is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps -- Your Honour, it seems it's more significant to Mr. Krajisnik to hear it. Perhaps when we're confident that we're in a position, perhaps after a break, to play it quickly, we can interject at that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that has been played before. Nothing is spoken which appears on the transcript, but of course the other issue is whether Mr. Krajisnik said anything in addition to that when the interview was recorded. And if you have a solution for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, he's keen to -- here we go maybe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that they do not have the transcript so they cannot work off the transcript directly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... which we can cover with the transparent sheet on which the territories are exactly marked, which is possessed by our Army, that those in fact are areas that belong to our people. A map, similar to this, as far as I am informed, was offered in Geneva, and it was made clear that Serbs want that the border of our country be ... that is the Neretva River Valley, and that is mostly territory of Republika Srpska. Knowing that we allow that there are certain enclaves on our territory that may be populated with the other ethnic communities. Sarajevo is a separate problem. At the moment, it is marked as ... the area of the city proper is marked as future Muslim territory, but we shall work for demilitarisation and division between the two ethnic communities, primarily Serbian and Muslim, and maybe a municipality for ... I mean, municipality populated by the Croatian community. Territory of the Republic of Republika Srpska represents in fact the border belong the Una River, the Sava River, with a small area that is not yet under our forces, I mean, it is not liberated yet. That is Orasje, that is the border, this is the territory of Semberija, of Ozren, and territory of Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. We presented, as our territory, to the Croatian community in Graz, that our border should be between our two ethnic communities that would be the Neretva River. In any case, this continuity of our territory, it is ... it is in one piece, if I may say so, and we will do our best that there is one constituent unit of Republika Srpska, and we shall allow the possibility of more constituent units of the Croatian and Muslim people. Simply, that is not a precondition. What is a precondition is that our Republic should be integral, and not divided into several parts."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say we do our best to help the interpreters. I'm assured that, although it's a bit late now, the transcript is in the clip of documents they were given before the start of the session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not in the English booth. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we do our best, Your Honour. I don't know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you have some comment to add, having heard the clip?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just now I listened to this text that was so fast, and I know that when I was listening to this in this same room I remember hearing the soundtrack with this break. Could I please have the tape and I can identify where the break is and where this sentence was left out? Right now I couldn't notice it because it was extremely fast, the text went extremely fast, and I know what it was that I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there -- is there an opportunity to -- during the next break, that if Mr. Krajisnik is returned a bit earlier to the courtroom that he could re-hear and review the -- this -- this video clip so that he could identify where there is a break? I didn't notice one, but it could be. If, of course, there should be a break, then, in the gestures and the movement of -- or if Mr. Sladojevic can --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can play it on my computer here then, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the security is invited to see if there is a possibility to have Mr. Krajisnik a bit earlier in court so he can see again and there is no need to make that part of that recording part of the hearing because it's not part of the trial but just for the information of Mr. Krajisnik. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, on the -- you've given some explanation of that, but on the fairly straightforward point of whether the Bosnian Serb army was, at the time of this television programme, possessing territories ethnically populated by other national communities, were there in fact within the area occupied by the army some such territories?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it's perfectly clear to everyone in this room that in 1992 Srebrenica and Zepa were - how should I put this? - were not held by the Army of Republika Srpska. That cannot be seen on this sheet. Perhaps this was made later, perhaps it was drawn in a different way and handed in as a map in Geneva. But this is not the border that was held by the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska. That is very easy to establish. It was only in 1995 that our forces took Srebrenica. After all, this is part of a case before this Court. So that confused me a bit. I know this entire interview, and I know how it went, but I cannot remember the time. I see that I was young and that my hair was dark, but I don't know when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, during the course of 1992, did the Bosnian Serb army take territories that had been majority occupied by other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, a similar question was one put -- once put by the Presiding Judge, but he phrased it differently. I'll try to answer your question, though, and, by your leave, I should like to give an answer that is fairly similar to what you just said now. The Army of Republika Srpska was fighting - if I can put it that way - with the other side and the situation changed very often. The territory that was held by the Army of Republika Srpska was much bigger in 1992 than it was at the end of the war. However, there were many changes in the territory. There was a front line, and then it depended on whether there was a clash at the front line and who pushed who away. Most often this was handled by the local commanders, depending on the situation. I don't know what -- what happened, when, and who would have what, but very few changes took place from the beginning of the war until 1995, when there was a problem with Srebrenica and Zepa. Practically the entire area was more or less - well, how should I put this? - the situation was the same. Now I can answer the other question, too. So what the army took - I mean the people in 1992 - except for a few changes, like the corridor, practically all the way up to 1995 until the case of Srebrenica and Zepa, that was it, you can see it on the maps. In Sarajevo changes were minor, and in all other areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't done this before, but it seems appropriate in this circumstance, and whatever questions Mr. Krajisnik was answering did not include the question that was asked by Mr. Stewart. I would say it's non-responsive, and it's up to the Court, of course, and Mr. Stewart as well, but I bring that to everyone's attention and I think the question and/or questions asked should be the ones responded to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I take it that you solicited an answer in your question from Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's not a -- it's not a topic which I propose to leave alone until the very end of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll -- you'll put that question again to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In some form or another, Your Honour. It's not a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't suit me to leave it dangling in the air, but I'm perfectly happy to deal with it now. That seems to be the most convenient thing. I was going to come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you see the point. You gave some sort of explanation, but the essential question whether during that year, 1992, the Bosnian Serb army did take territories that had been majority occupied by other ethnic groups, that question remains.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave an answer. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. The army was established on the 12th of May. Before that, a large part of the territory, that is to say the armed people on both sides, separated, and the army made slight corrections from its formation up until 1995. Zvornik happened, Bijeljina happened, and everything else, except for the corridor. And I have already given an answer, and that is that when the army was established, all it had was the problem of the corridor. In Sarajevo the situation in April was what it was, Vlasenica was what it was, and so was Zvornik, all before the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska, which means that the armed people had already set up borders before that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, I think as a matter of fact what we'd like to know is whether when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, whether they took or continued to exercise control over territories that were before the conflict inhabited by a Muslim majority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat: Certain corrections of the border were made, and those corrections were that a smaller portion of the territory where the Muslims were, and Serbs as well, that the army broke through the corridor in Konjevic Polje, for example, or things like that. But there weren't any major moves, large-scale moves, as there had been in April - that would be in line with that answer - except for the corridor. The army did not make any large-scale interventions because all the battles -- these battles took place before the army was established, and you can see that on the basis of the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have not carefully listened to my answer [sic] because I was referring to the -- whether the army kept or took. "Kept" means that it was taken already by armed forces before, but territories which were, by majority, inhabited by Muslims before the armed conflict; not whether what exactly changed after that. But once the Army of Republika Srpska was established, did they control territories which originally, that is before the outbreak of the armed conflict, that were by majority inhabited by Muslims? And I'm not talking about one village but a bit larger area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that the army received -- well, it won certain portions and lost others during that period of time. If we look at it unilaterally, the positive side is that it took some territories. These were minor corrections, though, compared to the situation that the army found on the ground when it was established. All the main operations had been completed before the army was established, except for the corridor. So the army did have control of certain regions and it lost others; it gained some and lost some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it did have control of certain regions by majority inhabited by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't understand your question, actually. If you want an answer, then my answer is yes, but I don't think that's the real answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to create a total picture, Mr. Krajisnik. This was just, perhaps, part of a picture but the subject of the question. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, I didn't understand Mr. Stewart's question because he didn't pose it in the proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's go to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you were asked by His Honour Judge Orie whether the Bosnian Serb army had control of certain regions by majority inhabited by Muslims. That was the question. And you said: Well, you didn't understand. Your answer was: Yes, but you didn't think that was the real answer. So what is the real answer, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Krajisnik, you've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to see whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understand -- from what I understand, Mr. Krajisnik, I do understand that you say don't put such a unilaterally oriented question to me, but rather ask me what the totality was. And you said: We gained some and we lost some. And by saying you gained some, I understood that the armed forces -- not major changes having been made after the Republika army had been established, you gained control of some areas which were by majority inhabited by Muslims, whereas you lost others. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, why did I say I didn't understand? Well, that's another question you've just asked. Mr. Stewart asked whether the army won over territory, whereas you asked whether it held control of the territory that the armed people had gained before that. Yes, it did. It had control of that. It was a territory where the Muslims had been previously. So I was a bit confused by the two aspects of the question. It didn't leave Vlasenica, Zvornik, and so on, it safe-guarded those territories which, prior to that, had been inhabited by a majority Muslim population. That's why I said that I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you remember that Mr. Okun gave evidence; it was a rather long time ago now in this trial. The -- I'm going to ask you about a number of things that Mr. Okun said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I indicated, Your Honour, that a lot of the transcript of Mr. Okun's evidence would be needed today. He gave evidence starting on the 22nd of June, 2004, and I'm going first to page 4152, which was in his evidence in chief. And he was asked if he accepted a generally -- his diaries which he produced reflecting approximately 50 to 60 meetings with members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. And then he went on, at the top of page 4153, to say that although he hadn't counted them, it was put to him that he'd had more than 25 meetings that included you, and he said there were certainly many, many meetings of varying lengths. Is a figure of something like 25 meetings that Mr. Okun attended, including you, is that in the right range of the number of meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, he was talking about the overall period.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that, as far as I remember, I met Mr. Okun -- or rather, saw Mr. Okun only once, and I think that was in Geneva, or perhaps London. I'm not quite sure. But I remember him well. He was Mr. Vance's assistant, and at those joint meetings he did attend, but how much, how many times, I don't know, but not in 1992. In 1992, as far as I recall, there was just one meeting, or perhaps two. But at those meetings, I didn't speak a single word to him. I attended the session. I don't think I took the floor either. So I cannot confirm anything about this. I don't think Mr. Okun was right when he said that. I couldn't have had a meeting with Mr. Okun. Far from it; no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He said at page 4165 - this is of the transcript - he was asked whether in the discussions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just looked over the question. So there's no confusion - and I know Mr. Stewart tried to clarify this - the question was whether the reference was to 1992. Mr. Stewart clarified that it wasn't limited to 1992, but included, for example, without saying so, 1993. And then it was difficult to tell whether Mr. Krajisnik was limiting his answer to 1992, and if he was, then I would again -- it's either a misunderstanding or it's non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there -- the only thing we should do at this moment when there's any misunderstanding -- Mr. Krajisnik, the question related to part of the testimony of Mr. Okun. It was read to you -- at least, it was summarised to you. When the question was put to you, you asked whether Mr. Stewart was referring to 1992, and then Mr. Stewart said Mr. Okun -- or at least he, that is Mr. Okun, was talking about the overall period. Did you include in your answer where you said no more than two, have you included 1993? And if not, could you tell us please whether that would change your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speaking about the entire period, because Mr. Stewart's question was quite clear, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- Mr. Okun indicated that it was really from early 1993 that the -- the frequency of these talks increased and they became intensive. Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993 you had the Vance-Owen Plan up until May when everything was completed with respect to our Assembly. So all the meetings took place during that period of time, the ones that Mr. Okun refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, he refers in his evidence - at page 4157, that is - to the Bosnian Serb wartime goals. And what he says is this -- he was asked at the middle of that page, by Mr. Tieger, Mr. Tieger said: "... you indicated that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were firm advocates of the Bosnian Serb political objectives, their wartime goals. Can you tell the Chamber now, please, what you understood those political objectives or wartime goals to be?" And then there was a technical hitch, and then he continued: "Yes. All the parties to the conflict, of course the three parties had goals. The Bosnian Serb wartime goals, as they were enunciated to us directly - and publicly as well - were six." And then he describes them. And it's not an elaborate description, Mr. Krajisnik, so I'll read it. "First --" well, I'll stop at each one and ask you whether you agree that it was a Bosnian Serb wartime goal. "First, to have their own state, Republika Srpska juridical state." Do you agree with what Mr. Okun says, that that was one of the Bosnian Serb wartime goals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with the whole observation of Mr. Okun. They weren't wartime goals; they were political goals which he didn't understand because he hadn't taken part in the previous negotiations. And we only spoke about political goals at the conference, not wartime goals. We were discussing the conference. Now, had the goal been political for the negotiators, that we should have our own Republika Srpska, that is true because that was a precondition from beginning to end, from the start of the negotiating process to the end. So that was the political goal, but not the war goal, wartime goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the second was that the state, that is Republika Srpska, clearly, "was to have continuous territory and to be contiguous with Serbia, not chopped up, patches." Now, again, Mr. Krajisnik, was that a wartime goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In negotiations we kept repeating our starting positions, and one of those was the corridor that I explained to you. And he mentions this in one part. We asked that it -- that Republika Srpska be a whole, in one block, because by exchange of territory we could arrive at that goal. But that was a political proposal in the commission that he was a member of on the part of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the -- the third one, he says: "Third, to be ethnically pure Serb or overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb as they could make it ..." Now, was that a wartime goal of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was never a goal, and you can see that from all the documents, that the prime goal discussed was separation to form Republika Srpska where the majority of the population were Serbs, then a Muslim republic where the majority were Muslims, a Croatian one where the majority were Croats. But of course there would be other ethnic groups living there, too, and this was not discussed in any of the talks. No mention was made of any kind of pure territory. So that was quite impossible. It wouldn't have been appropriate to discuss things like that at meetings of that kind, let alone realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And: "Fourth, to have a special relationship with Yugoslavia or Serbia as the case may be." Was that a wartime goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not only about war. We got agreement from the Muslim side and the international community. They agreed that we can have special relationships with the neighbouring republics. Ask the Croats, the Muslims, all the three ethnic communities, that they can create and forge special relationships. Everything that wouldn't challenge the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that's what that was about. He probably defined it in a different way, and I'm sure he must have understood it wrongly, and that is what was gained in the Dayton Agreement. Everything, all the agreements, all this was stipulated in all the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then: "Fifth, to divide Sarajevo into a Muslim and a Bosnian Serb section." Was that a wartime goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always our goal not to be expelled from Sarajevo, so we wanted to have the peripheral parts of Sarajevo, to have our local administration there. We never sought, in figurative terms, to erect Berlin Walls anywhere. What we wanted to see was the transformation of Sarajevo where certain parts and districts would form separate municipalities where the Serbs would be the majority population. And there are documents to back that up, documents from contemporaneous documents about the proposals that were put forward for Sarajevo, and they were along the lines of what I've just told you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then: "Sixth and last, to have a veto power over any residual powers that would be held by the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." Was that a wartime goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not one of the goals. It was a point, an item, advocated by all three sides. And from the very beginning there was discussion about the fact that certain items and issues should be resolved by consensus in -- on other issues, you had to have a four-fifths majority so as not to jeopardise the national interests at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that was the position taken by all three sides, and that exists in Bosnia-Herzegovina today. In all the agreements, that was provided for. It wasn't just a Serb proposal; it was an issue that we discussed, an item on the agenda that we discussed, and that was incorporated into all the agreements. It wasn't a veto; it was a way in which -- by which to solve the situation and to avoid violations in the constitution and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Okun said in his evidence that those six Bosnian Serb wartime goals, as he said they were, had been enunciated to him and his colleagues in those negotiations directly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. He must have heard that there were six strategic goals, and now he attempted to formulate this and highlight questions that were often mentioned in negotiations when Mr. Vance was present, and Mr. Owen as well, the co-presidents of the conference, but that was never formulated as goals, they were just issues that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm getting a bit lost. Mr. Krajisnik, in one of your earlier answers you said Mr. Okun was not correct when he said he had up to 25 meetings which included you. You said: "I don't think Mr. Okun was right when he said that. I couldn't have had a meeting with Mr. Okun. Far from it, no." Now you were asked about what was told to Mr. Okun during these negotiations, and you quite clearly say that this could not have been said to him. I'm -- when you said that Mr. Okun was not right, did you intend to say that you had no meetings with him, which is not the same as what he said, because he was talking about meetings that included you, which might be something different from a direct meeting with you. Is that what you meant? Or did you mean to say: Well, it may well be that Mr. Okun has been present during a meeting some 25 times where I was present as well. Since you're quite explicit on what was not said to Mr. Okun, could you clarify this for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There could not have been, theoretically speaking, 25 meetings that I attended with Mr. Okun throughout his participation in the conference because there weren't that many days, there weren't that many meetings between us. He was there from the beginning of 1993 until May or June. He wasn't there later on; later on it was Owen and Stoltenberg. So what I'm saying is that as far as I recollect, there could not have been that many meetings. Now what I'm saying now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I interrupt you. How many, approximately, could it have been; ten, 15, 20? Because you say it's not 25 -- couldn't have been 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I'm telling you is this: I cannot give you an exact number. I can't guess. But 25 is much too many. I can't say whether it was two or three or five, but I tell you the time period when he was there, and I can find out exactly when we had a meeting with him, from January until the end of April, until the Athens meeting, and then Mr. Okun was no longer there, nor was Mr. Vance in 1993. And there was one meeting in 1992. So I'm trying to tell you this. Now, whether it was five, six, seven meetings, I don't know, but 25 is much too high a figure. And I can answer the other question as well, if you're interested in hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you did not attend all of the meetings, of course we ask ourselves how could you know what was not said during these negotiations to Mr. Okun -- or at least to those who attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain what I meant. If there was a visit to Geneva, for example, and if there are a number of meetings during that visit to Geneva, perhaps three, four, five, six meetings, that might have been what Mr. Okun was counting, with other people attending; Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Karadzic perhaps. Then, possibly, there could have been more meetings than I know about. Are you following me? I didn't sit down to a meeting with him where he was present. If I was to say two or three times, that, too, would be guesswork on my part. So quite possibly he meant one meeting, one visit to Geneva, with a number of meetings within that one visit. And that's something else again, because there were discussions held all day; bilateral, separate meetings, held in the morning, held in the afternoon, but I count that as one meeting, the Geneva meeting, although we might have spent a whole day's discussing and putting forward various proposals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you consider it possible that your colleagues at a -- your Bosnian Serb colleagues at a meeting which you were not present enunciated those six wartime goals as Mr. Okun had described them in his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite convinced that goals formulated in that way could not have been presented; however, what is possible is this: During a conference or a meeting scheduled in Geneva, for example, if we had an issue, one issue, several issues or questions, and if Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic had been with him and with Mr. Vance and had separate meetings, perhaps they might have put forward their attitudes and positions with respect to certain issues: We want to have a united territory, we want to avoid out-voting, we want this and that. So that he might have considered to be our strategic goals, but that was in the course of formulating a concept on how to achieve a peace agreement. There were no official goals that he was presenting; that's what I said. Quite simply, when you discuss things, you look at different variants, how to solve problems, the problem of the corridor, the problem of Republika Srpska, and things like that. And his main task - that's why he remembered this - his commission's main task was not to have Republika Srpska and to abolish something that we had agreed upon, the basic things we had agreed upon. And that's why he remembered that as being our goals, and it was our goal indeed to be consistent in persevering what we had started from the very beginning and what the international community had agreed to, but that didn't suit him because he didn't want to see that happen. And they proposed that Republika Srpska should not be incorporated into the Vance-Owen Plan, and that's why it was rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, one of the things Mr. Okun said, and this is found at page 4165 of the transcript, he was asked by Mr. Tieger: "Ambassador Okun, was one of the issues of considerable significance, perhaps central significance during the course of these negotiations, the amount of territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Bosnian Serbs laid claim to?" And he said: "Yes." Mr. Krajisnik, is -- if the same question is put to you, is your answer yes or no or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In this case - I know it wasn't intentional - I think it would be helpful to read the entire response.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would and I was going to, but I was going to do that as a separate question, Your Honour, which is a legitimate way of approaching it, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, at this point -- the question then was: Was one of the issues of considerable significance, perhaps central significance, during the negotiations the amount of territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina that you, the Bosnian Serbs, laid claim to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The size of the territory was not the question that was of crucial importance as far as the Serb side was concerned; however, the question of territories was the only question and the most important question during the peace process. It was only the maps that were a problem; everything else was easy to resolve. We were prepared to have joint maps made, regardless of the actual size of the land involved and regardless of the situation on the front line. We just wanted to have a peaceful separation and three constituent units. It wasn't the size of the territory that mattered to us, 64 per cent or whatever, but to have it done through peaceful means. And that can be seen on the basis of all these plans, that we even reduced our territory to 50 per cent, later on it turned out to be 40 per cent, and that shows exactly how ready we were to withdraw from territories and all that. You will see that not in the Owen-Stoltenberg plan but in Mr. Owen's book, that we agreed to all these maps. So there is no dilemma as far as that is concerned. Of course we were prepared to accept even smaller territories. It was only about territories that the sides were having a dispute on, to know where the separation line would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see, having answered that question in the affirmative himself, he said, yes, it had been one of the issues of considerable significance during the negotiations, Mr. Okun continued. He said that was another constant refrain, and they - that's you, the Bosnian Serbs - they had a formula for it. It went this way: We are 35 per cent of the people, but we own 65 per cent of the land. Now, was that a formula or a constant negotiating point that you, the Bosnian Serbs, were putting forward in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the arguments of the Serb side. When we say that we have to get a territory that would exceed the figure of 30 per cent, which was the population figure. The population cannot be the only criterion, but territory, too. Our territory, where the Serbs lived, is primarily rural with very few towns. All the industries and all the big towns are in Muslim-held territory. Quantity is not the same as quality, and that was our argument when we were trying to explain why there should be a disproportion with regard to territory, why the Serb side should have more territory. That is why the Serb side actually got 49 per cent, half of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the rural part, whereas the central part, the richest part, was what the Muslim federation -- the Muslim-Croat federation got.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he said that, "We heard it repeatedly that this formula," as he described it -- I think that was his word. Yes, formula of 35 per cent of the people, 65 per cent of the land, he said: "We heard it repeatedly from Mr. Milosevic. We heard it from Dr. Karadzic. We heard it from Mr. Krajisnik, Koljevic, Buha, all of them." Is it correct that they heard it from, among other people, you, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they heard it from me the way I had put it, and I heard it from experts. I didn't do the measuring. I heard it from experts, this 64 per cent, the experts who drew this map, that the Serbs own 64 per cent of the land of Bosnia-Herzegovina; forests, meadows, fields, whereas the central part is the most densely populated and that is where the predominant population is Muslim and Croat. And in percentage terms, that's less. Probably he could have heard this from me; I don't exclude that possibility. I'm not saying that I said it, but I do not exclude the possibility that I did say that Serbs, in terms of the land, have 64 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of what experts in this field say. Now, whether that is correct or not, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, there's a short passage I'm just going to read but not ask you a question, Mr. Krajisnik, because otherwise one doesn't understand the bit I am coming to for a question. But on page 4166, 4166 of the transcript, after this answer about territories and the formula, Mr. Okun was asked by Mr. Tieger: "Was the genocide committed against the Serbs during World War II raised in the context of the enunciation of the amount of territory to which Bosnian Serbs were allegedly entitled?" To which he answered: "Yes. That was also a factor." And then a page or two on - it's 4167 of the transcript, line 20 - Mr. Tieger asked: "Ambassador Okun, with regard to your previous answer about the emphasis on the genocide of World War II, did that mean that Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and the other Bosnian Serb leaders asserted a claim to territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina on which non-Serbs were a majority and Serbs were a minority?" And his answer to that was: "Yes. They made that explicit." Is that correct, Mr. Krajisnik? Again, I come to the rest of the answer in a moment, but is that correct that you, among others, made it explicit that you asserted a claim to territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina on which Serbs were a minority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. That is not true because we were consistently saying, from the beginning to the end, that Serb territories should be where Serbs are a majority. If this were to be possible, it could only be achieved through an exchange of territories, when we agree on that. So if some territories where Muslims are a majority come to belong to the Serbs, and vice versa, then we would try to apply to principle, but it's not that we have the right. In the talks, there were proposals to that effect, especially our talks with the Croat [Realtime transcript read in error "Muslim"] side: You cede this to us, and we will cede that to you. It is a well-known fact what is traditionally Croat and what is traditionally Serb. So this was the other principle that was also very important when we started working on the maps from the very beginning. It's not that we were saying, say, Zvornik is ours. No. Zvornik is majority, and that is what I can say. If somebody says: Well, why did you take Zvornik? I can give an answer to that, too. So if we analyse things from the beginning to the end, everything can be established why things happened, but this one principle where there -- where one people is a majority, that is their territory, and where the second people is a majority, that's their territory, and where the third people is a majority, that is their territory, and then we can work on the establishment of these constituent units in that way. Well, that did not suit them because Mr. Okun and Mr. Vance didn't like that, and they gave up on the Republika Srpska, and then we didn't like that because we had already -- we had already given up on Yugoslavia because we were promised a Republika Srpska. And now we were being denied a Republika Srpska, too. That is what he didn't understand because he hadn't been there from day one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Krajisnik said he could answer the question why they had taken Zvornik. Could you try to do that in five to ten lines, Mr. Krajisnik, why Zvornik, although being a majority Muslim inhabited municipality, why it was taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just, before it goes off the screen, just clear up a point. At line 12, which is going to go off the screen in a minute, it says: "Especially our talks at the Muslim side," and Mr. Sladojevic assures me that it was Croat that was said there. And Mr. Krajisnik is nodding. So may we make that correction. I'm sorry to interrupt Your Honour there, but otherwise it goes off the screen and it's a nuisance then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you've been asked by His Honour to try to say in five or ten lines why Zvornik was taken although being a majority Muslim-inhabited municipality.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honourable Judge Orie, about ten or 15 days ago, put a question whether Republika Srpska or the Serb leadership thought that Zvornik belonged to Republika Srpska, because it was taken by the army, it was taken by paramilitary formations. The answer is as follows: There was one situation before the outbreak of the war. Before the beginning of the war, talks were held, negotiations were held, on the division of Zvornik into two municipalities. I have documents about that, and the Serb part of the municipality, that is to say the Serb local communities, is what the Serb side thought that they had a right to, not the urban part of Zvornik, where they did not have a majority. And these negotiations that were held -- well, I mean the local leadership agreed on this. And then the Muslims set up barricades and this initiative first came from them, and all the Serbs fled from Zvornik. And then Arkan called the leadership to Mali Zvornik, I learned about that later, and he slapped all of them around and said: Why did you allow the Muslims to deceive you? And then they took all of Zvornik. That did not mean that in the negotiations when we were negotiating we had to disregard taken territories. I must assure you that Mr. Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg were on a terrace at Lake Zvornik when that question was discussed, and we said that we would be interested in exchanging territories with the Muslim side to get Zvornik on our map because we needed for the corridor. But that was not a precondition by our authorities because somebody had taken all of Zvornik. That is to say we simply wanted that part of Zvornik which was ethnically Serb. That is the whole truth with regard to Zvornik, Vlasenica, and I don't know what other municipalities; however, once the war broke out, that was a different matter. But according to the maps, the Muslims had the right to those territories in Zvornik where the Muslims had a majority. The Serbs did not have a majority there, and that was it. And we could not have had a corridor if we could not reach agreement on this and if we did not agree through the international community, too, so nobody has the right to say, "This is my territory" if another people are a majority there. You can only reach agreement if there is mutual consent, and that was the philosophy from day one. Mr. Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg were on a terrace in Zvornik. There is this restaurant there and we were sitting there and talking precisely about that problem. And the Muslim side, afterwards, accepted that the -- that Zvornik should belong to the Serb side because they were looking for other parts when we were working on maps. It's not that we said: Ah, we are 20 per cent there -- or actually there's 46 per cent of us -- rather, 36 per cent, I'm sorry, and we didn't say, But we want all of this to belong to us. No, no one has the right to take someone else's territory. You have a territory, then you can exchange it, you can reach agreements on the basis of the priorities you have. That's the way it was. That was the principle from the beginning to the end. It's not that that was it, but certain principles were established and we had to abide by that, and I'm saying what the international community, the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs knew when the talks were being conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I invited you for five or ten lines because if you give very long answers, there will be less time for additional questions to be put to you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. I'm also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry. I think I spoke temperamentally. Mr. President, I do apologise. I should have spoken less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please. Yes, we'll adjourn until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had a bit of a late start. That's due to the fact that the Judges wanted to deliberate on the request for more further time from Defence. The decision will be delivered today orally. I was informed that the review of the CD-ROM was not successful -- DVD video. If a copy could be made by the Defence, nothing else on it, so that Mr. Krajisnik could look at it in his cell, fine. Otherwise, next break, new chances, I would say, to be successful -- but I take it if it's on a CD-ROM or a DVD, that it could be easily copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can easily do that, I'm sure, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, during the negotiations -- and I'm talking about the -- the later negotiations in which Mr. Okun was involved, did you, the Bosnian Serbs, did you seek to recover in those negotiations territories which you regarded as having been lost to Serbs during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we did not ask for those territories, but in various talks, at Assemblies, when different maps were drawn, and perhaps even in talks with various representatives, we presented this problem of the ethnic structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially certain areas, had changed because of the genocide against the Serbs during the Second World War. That was one reason. So it's not that it was that important a reason in the drawing of the maps, but in the talks it was important and this was done with the aim of obtaining a better position in the negotiating process. We did the maps on the basis of the census that was carried out after the Second World War; '71, '81, '91, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is at page 4168 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- the -- Mr. Okun had made a note in relation to a comment by Dr. Karadzic that, as he recorded it: "Muslims want the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina: High birth rate." And he was asked by Mr. Tieger: "Was the reference to the alleged birth rate of the Muslims a reference that was unique to a particular meeting in question or was it a recurring theme?" And he said it was a recurring theme. And then in his next answer, he said: "The Bosnian Serb leadership held steadily to the point of view that they needed their own Republika Srpska with their own ruling institutions in order to ward off majoritarian rule by the Bosnian Muslims ..." and I won't bother with the rest of the answer, Mr. Krajisnik, because my question is: Did you in those negotiations, those talks, mention or raise the question of the Muslim birth rate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was mentioned during the course of the negotiations. That's a fact. But that was of secondary importance, not primary importance. It was mentioned that the Muslims had a higher birth rate, higher than the other two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then - and this is 4169 of the transcript - Mr. Okun was asked: "And was the emphasis on the number of Muslims who would live within territories held or occupied by Bosnian Serbs a matter of recurring interest to the Bosnian Serb leadership?" And he said: "No. They didn't emphasise that so much because they knew what they were doing. They were removing Muslims from the territory. It was happening, they knew it. They were ordering -- I mean they were in charge of it, so they were aiming to make their future Republika Srpska as ethnically pure as they could. This was one of their six goals, and they made no secret of that fact, but of course they didn't advertise it either." Mr. Krajisnik, at -- at any time when you were engaged in continuing talks in which Mr. Okun was also engaged, was it the position that you, the Bosnian Serb leadership, were removing Muslims from territory or causing them to be removed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect. I don't know how Mr. Okun could come to that conclusion. We never said that, not at a single meeting that I attended, and where I know that my colleagues attended, too, along with them. In all talks it was quite clear that everybody should return to their homes, and that was our objective, and we agreed on that in every one of these agreements that was made, not to remove anyone by force. That was not the policy and we never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My question was very strictly different, Mr. Krajisnik, which was not whether you said it but whether it was, in fact, happening. Could you answer that question in those specific terms, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the knowledge I had, it was -- well, knowledge. I mean what I managed to hear from my colleagues and what they said publicly, that these were voluntary departures of the Muslims, that they were exercising their right to the freedom of movement. I don't know on what conditions people from the municipalities who testified here left, but I heard this same story that was presented here from Serbs, too, Serb witnesses who appeared before this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then further on in the transcript, it was actually the following day, 23rd of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for one clarification. Only on the first part of your answer, Mr. Krajisnik. You said you heard from your colleagues and what they said publicly. Who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard the statement of Mr. Karadzic after the meeting with Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen in Banja Luka. "There is no ethnic cleansing in our parts. We allow the freedom of movement." I heard that when he returned, too, when he returned to Pale. That's what I heard. It was made in public, that statement. It's in the newspapers, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware of the numbers, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I knew nothing of that phenomenon. I'm just saying that I heard this in general terms. I know about the Muslims leaving Pale and I can talk about that; as for the rest, I didn't know who left how and in which way and from which areas and whether they actually left at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- you said: "I heard this same story that was presented here from Serbs, too, Serb witnesses who appeared before this court." What did they tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb witnesses said that Muslims put forth requests that they wanted to leave and that they were leaving voluntarily. That is what I heard later, I'm saying later, that there were departures of Muslims. And before I got here, I never heard of expulsions of Muslims, but here I heard Muslim witnesses stating that they had been expelled. But now I'm talking about my own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that before you arrived in The Hague you never heard about expulsion of Muslims, Mr. Krajisnik, not from 1995 up till the moment that you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assure you, Mr. President, from every municipality from where Muslims left, whoever I talked to in the following years, everybody told me that Muslims wanted to leave and that they left voluntarily. I never heard from a single local official that they said that they had expelled Muslims. I'm talking about something that was perhaps a rare topic of conversation. But that there were population movements, I knew that. And I knew that that happened throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I did not hear of anyone expelling anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You now limit your source of knowledge as local officials. Did you hear any such story from others than, perhaps, these local officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me about up until 1995, whether I had heard of expulsions of Muslims. I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me about before that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you about until your arrival in The Hague, because that was your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could you please be clearer, and then I'm going to give you an answer. Could you just tell me what the question is that I'm supposed to answer. I told you about what I knew up until 1995, and now you're asking me whether I heard about it from somebody else. Tell me who this somebody else is and then I'm going to tell you, gladly, who I heard what from. But who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, your testimony is on the transcript as saying: "And before I got here, I never heard of expulsion of Muslims, but here I heard Muslim witnesses stating that they had been expelled. But now I'm talking about my own knowledge." Then I asked you whether it was your testimony that before you arrived in The Hague, because the word "here" expressed twice, I understood that as here, in The Hague, I asked you whether you -- whether it was your testimony that before you arrived in The Hague that you never heard about expulsion of Muslims. And I added to that: "Not from 1995 up till the moment that you were arrested," so that's after the conflict. And then in your answer you said: "Everybody told me that Muslims wanted to leave and that they left voluntarily. I never heard from a single local official that they said that they had expelled Muslims." And then I said: "But did you hear that from anyone else, perhaps, between 1995 up till your arrival in The Hague?" That's what I asked you. I thought it was a very clear question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking who you mean? Do you mean local officials or some objective foreigner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whoever. Whoever, Mr. Krajisnik. You said: "I never heard about it until my arrival in The Hague." Then I asked you, "Is it true that you tell us that you never heard that even after 1995?" And then you said, "I never heard it from local officials." My next question then was: "Did you hear it from anyone else since 1995?" I'm not saying by whom -- from whom, but I'm just asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm a mature person. I cannot be playing games of riddles. I'm going to tell you what I heard in 1993, 1994, 1995. I'm going to tell you that I heard the statements of Owen and Vance, and I heard what Mazowiecki, said, and when I asked my colleagues, the locals, whether that was true, they said: No, it's not true. That's the point of my answer. And then as for these people who were on the ground who were objective, they said: That is not correct. And I said that from them I did not hear that anybody had been expelled. There were Muslim statements about expulsions, there were different statements, but this is the point of my answer. I mean, I'm not used to this, whether I'm going to make a mistake in using a word or two. Just ask me and I'm going to tell you everything; what I heard, who I heard it from, whether I heard it from a president of a municipality or whatever. No, I did not hear it from a president of a municipality. They said that they left voluntarily. I heard Mazowiecki, I heard Vance, I heard Owen. I heard different statements from Muslims too, and so on and so forth. That's the truth, and that's why I'm saying that I'm afraid I'm going to fall into a trap. I don't want this to be like I'm in a quiz, and I want to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now understand your testimony to be that the internationals, to put it briefly, confronted you with accusations, allegations, of Muslims being removed, and you heard from your people that they only used their freedom of movement and they all voluntarily left. And your conclusion then was that your people were given the right information and the internationals gave you wrong information. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one slight correction: It wasn't the international representatives who confronted me with this, but I heard their statements in the media, in the newspapers. And I saw Karadzic's statement and Vance-Owen's, and I asked Karadzic which of this is correct, tell me. And he said it's not a correct what they say. I have a written report from the army that met with Vance and Owen at that time and they took pleasure in hearing them say positive things, and then they went to the Muslim side, sat down with them, and gained a different impression, saying that there was ethnic cleansing. So I have all this indirect information. And when I met some local representative, I don't know -- I can't say when I met local representatives, but anyway, they always spoke about the voluntary departure of Muslims. So that's why I say that I don't know that anybody was expelled. I have no direct knowledge of that because I was under the conviction that it was as I was told. I don't deny that it happened, but I'm just saying what my role was. It wasn't that Owen and Stoltenberg told me, and Vance, it was that Karadzic in Banja Luka told me about it, and I read it in the papers and I asked him, and he got his answers from the local structures as to whether this was correct or not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was never raised during any meeting with representatives of the international community at which you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there was some conference or other, then I don't exclude that at such conferences the question was on the agenda and a debate on the matter was held, and then various sides put forward pro and con arguments and I, as an observer, heard each side out. And when they went back, they would check it out, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, or I don't know who, and then they would receive information from the field saying that that wasn't the case, that the case was different, just like people testified here before the court. So that's the truth of it. Now, I don't say that this was not discussed at some conference, but it was denied by people who were well-informed, who received information, not me -- not I myself; I didn't receive any information or reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What newspaper did publish about these allegations made by the representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have the papers here. I've got them with me. Whether it was Glas, Srpski Glas, or the Politika Glas from Banja Luka or Politika, the daily from Belgrade. I don't know when I received it, but I know that I did read that somewhere there. And I can document that for you and show you the newspapers, and I can also provide you with the military report as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed. No ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the transcript reference now is 4187. Mr. Tieger asked: "Ambassador," Mr. Okun, "I would like to begin with something you raised in your testimony yesterday. In response to a question about the number of Muslims who would live within territories held by the Bosnian Serbs, you referred to the removal of Muslims from the territory and the ethnic cleansing of Muslims by the Bosnian Serb forces. First, can I ask you about the sources of information that you and the Secretary Vance and the other negotiators had concerning the ethnic cleansing of Muslims from territories within Bosnia-Herzegovina by Bosnian Serb forces?" And Mr. Okun's answer was: "The first indication, and it was official and written, came from the plebiscite that the Bosnian Serb Assembly ordered in November, 1991. There was a plebiscite of the Bosnian Serb people to decide whether to opt for remaining in a Bosnian Serb entity and also Yugoslavia. And one might have thought that there would be just a general plebiscite, you know, of the million and a quarter or so Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it was not organised that way. It was organised opstina by opstina. And a very important, significant aspect was the decision written into the rules of the plebiscite that in any opstina where more than 50 per cent of the Serbs voted in favour of Republika Srpska, regardless of the size of the opstina, regardless of their percentage in the opstina, that opstina became part of the Republika Srpska." Now, the -- Mr. Krajisnik, the answer hasn't finished yet, but I just want to ask you: So far, are you in agreement simply with Mr. Okun's description of how he understood the plebiscite to have worked?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His conclusion was erroneous, Mr. Okun's, as to the goal of why the -- or the reason why the plebiscite was organised. I can explain that to you, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we'll take it in stages, Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, his description of the mechanics of the plebiscite, do you agree that he's got that correct, without going any further?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't give the right description. The plebiscite has -- had as its goal that the Serbs, and the others, should state their views to say whether they thought Bosnia should remain in Yugoslavia or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, as far as this specific bit is concerned he said: "A significant aspect was that it was written into the rules of the plebiscite that in any opstina where more than 50 per cent of Serbs voted in favour of Republika Srpska, that opstina," however many Serbs there were there, "became part of Republika Srpska." Was that technically a correct description of the way the plebiscite worked?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the correct description.
